title: Birbal and the Cook
summary: The royal cook serves oversalted soup to the Emperor. Birbal uses an amusing salt test to help the cook correct his recipe without fear.
full_text:
The imperial head cook, Mir Baqir, had prepared meals for Emperor Akbar for fifteen years without a flaw. However, on a sweltering afternoon, overwhelmed by heat and distracted by his daughter's illness, the cook accidentally added salt twice to the Emperor's favorite saffron mutton broth.

When Akbar took his first spoonful in the private dining chamber, his face darkened with disgust: 'Ugh! This soup is like seawater! It is poisoned with salt!'

Akbar spat the broth onto the floor and shouted for the guards: 'Drag that incompetent cook here! He shall be stripped of his position and thrown into the dungeons!'

Birbal, who was dining with the Emperor, quickly tasted a drop of the broth from his own spoon. Seeing that the mistake was an honest accident, Birbal stepped in:

'Sire, allow me to question the cook. In ancient Persian culinary art, there is a rare medical reason why a master chef adds double salt.'

Curious, Akbar halted the guards. Mir Baqir was brought into the room, trembling and weeping with terror.

Birbal asked the cook solemnly: 'Mir Baqir, tell His Majesty the truth: did you oversalt this soup because you have developed a secret love affair, or because you were trying to preserve the Emperor's humors from the summer heat?'

The cook blinked in bewilderment, then fell to his knees: 'Neither, my lord! My mind was shattered because my youngest daughter is burning with a high fever at home, and in my sorrow, my hand slipped and I salted the cauldron twice! Forgive me, Sire, kill me if you must, but spare my poor child!'

Akbar's anger melted into sympathy.

Birbal smiled at the Emperor: 'Sire, salt can ruin a broth, but sorrow ruins a father's mind. The salt was an error of grief, not malice.'

Akbar ordered the imperial royal physician dispatched immediately to treat the cook's daughter with royal medicines, granted the cook three days of leave, and ordered a simple fresh broth prepared. Mir Baqir bowed with tears of gratitude, and Akbar thanked Birbal for transforming royal rage into compassionate mercy.
